Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.
:::

## In 60 seconds

Before and during an ablation, images give the mapping system a shape to work on: the left atrium
outlined on CT or MRI, scar or fibrosis marked in its wall, or a shell built from intracardiac
echo. Networks now draw these outlines. In an open benchmark of left atrial segmentation on
late-gadolinium MRI, the best method reached a Dice score of 93.2% and a mean surface distance of
0.7 mm [@xiong2020]. Whether such a number is good enough depends on the structure and on the use.
This module derives the metrics that judge a segmentation (Dice, Hausdorff distance, average
surface distance and normalized surface Dice), shows why the same 1-mm boundary error costs a thin
wall far more Dice than a blood pool, and introduces the concordance index used for risk models
built on images. The clinical correlate follows MRI-defined fibrosis from an association with
outcome to a randomized trial of fibrosis-guided ablation [@marrouche2014; @marrouche2022].

## From the field

- **Benchmarks set the language.** The 2018 Left Atrium Segmentation Challenge gave 27 teams 154
  late-gadolinium MRI volumes with labels from three experts; methods that first found a region of
  interest and then segmented it did better than single networks [@xiong2020]. In the Medical
  Segmentation Decathlon, the left atrium task had only 20 labelled training volumes, and methods
  were ranked by Dice and by a surface metric with a 4-mm tolerance for the heart
  [@antonelli2022]. The winning method, nnU-Net, configures itself for each new data set
  [@isensee2021].
- **Open tools from industry and academia.** MONAI, an open-source PyTorch framework for medical
  imaging, was initially led by NVIDIA and King's College London; it ships U-Nets, Dice losses and a
  loader for the Decathlon data [@cardoso2022monai]. Its labelling tool, MONAI Label, was shown on
  the Decathlon left atrium, where an expert needed about 10 minutes to outline one atrium by hand
  [@diazpinto2022monailabel]. Lab part F uses MONAI's U-Net when it is installed.
- **Shells from intracardiac echo.** One centre compared a deep-learning module that builds the
  left atrial shell from intracardiac echo with its earlier manual contouring: total procedure time
  122.5 against 129.0 minutes, and 1-year freedom from AF 80.0% against 81.4% (not significantly
  different), in a before-and-after design [@zou2026].
- **Thin walls.** CT measurements in 60 patients with persistent AF found a mean left atrial wall
  thickness of 1.89 mm, ranging from 0.5 to 3.5 mm [@beinart2011]. At that scale one voxel is a
  large share of the wall (demo m40-d2).
- **From images to risk.** A deep survival model on contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI predicted
  arrhythmic sudden death with a concordance index of 0.83 on internal validation and 0.74 on an
  independent test set [@popescu2022]. Stanford and King's College groups combined CT shape, deep
  image features and clinical data to predict AF recurrence after ablation (retrospective, nested
  cross-validation) [@razeghi2023].
- **How to test an imaging AI.** Stanford's EchoNet-Dynamic segmented the left ventricle on echo
  videos with a Dice of 0.92 and released 10,030 annotated videos [@ouyang2020]. Members of that team
  then ran a blinded, randomized trial of AI against sonographers for the first read of ejection fraction
  [@he2023]: a design that imaging AI in EP has rarely had.

## Derivations

Symbols: $P$ and $T$ the predicted and true regions (sets of voxels or points), $\lvert\cdot\rvert$
volume or area, $\partial P$ and $\partial T$ their surfaces, $d(x, \partial T)$ the distance from a
point to a surface, $\delta$ a boundary offset (mm), $S$ and $V$ surface area and volume, $R$ a
sphere radius, $t$ a wall thickness, $\tau$ a distance tolerance.

### Overlap

The **Dice coefficient** $2\lvert P\cap T\rvert/(\lvert P\rvert+\lvert T\rvert)$ was derived in
[m39](m39-ai-electrograms-maps.qmd#eq-m39-dice). Some papers report the **Jaccard index** (intersection
over union) $J = \lvert P\cap T\rvert/\lvert P\cup T\rvert$ instead. Since $\lvert P\cup T\rvert =
\lvert P\rvert + \lvert T\rvert - \lvert P\cap T\rvert$,

$$
\mathrm{Dice} = \frac{2J}{1 + J}, \qquad J = \frac{\mathrm{Dice}}{2 - \mathrm{Dice}}
$$ {#eq-m40-jaccard}

so the two rank methods identically, but $J$ is always the smaller number: $J = 0.8$ is a Dice of
0.889. Convert before comparing papers.

Overlap is blind to where errors lie. A stray island far from the atrium costs only its own
volume; a boundary error along a vein costs a lot of Dice for a small structure. The Decathlon
organizers noted that Dice suits large structures and is unstable for very small ones, where a few
voxels change the score [@antonelli2022; @reinke2024].

**Key takeaways**

- Dice and Jaccard carry the same information; convert with @eq-m40-jaccard before comparing.
- Overlap says how much, not where.

### Distances between surfaces

Distance metrics compare the two surfaces. The **Hausdorff distance** is the largest distance from
any point of one surface to the other:

$$
\mathrm{HD}(P, T) = \max\left\{ \max_{p \in \partial P} d(p, \partial T),\; \max_{q \in \partial T} d(q, \partial P) \right\}
$$ {#eq-m40-hausdorff}

Because it is a maximum, one island sets it. The **95th-percentile Hausdorff distance** (HD95)
replaces each maximum by the 95th percentile and ignores the worst 5% of points; toolkits differ in
whether they pool the two directions first, so check which one a paper used. The **average
symmetric surface distance** (ASSD) averages every distance:

$$
\mathrm{ASSD} = \frac{\int_{\partial P} d(p, \partial T)\, dp + \int_{\partial T} d(q, \partial P)\, dq}{\lvert\partial P\rvert + \lvert\partial T\rvert}
$$ {#eq-m40-assd}

On voxels the integrals become sums over surface voxels. The **normalized surface Dice** (NSD)
counts the share of both surfaces that lie within a tolerance $\tau$ of the other:

$$
\mathrm{NSD}_\tau = \frac{\lvert\{p \in \partial P : d(p, \partial T) \le \tau\}\rvert + \lvert\{q \in \partial T : d(q, \partial P) \le \tau\}\rvert}{\lvert\partial P\rvert + \lvert\partial T\rvert}
$$ {#eq-m40-nsd}

It asks the clinical question directly: how much of the outline is close enough? The tolerance is
a choice; the Decathlon used 4 mm for the heart, set with clinicians [@antonelli2022].

::: {.demo #m40-d1 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m40-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m40-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m40-d1-segmentation-metrics.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Two-dimensional discs and circles. Dice from the disc areas; HD, ASSD and NSD from
  @eq-m40-hausdorff, @eq-m40-assd and @eq-m40-nsd with distances between the outlines, weighted by
  arc length and integrated by the midpoint rule on 3,600 points (720 for the curves). The values
  match masks rasterized at 0.05 mm (`tests/test_m40_imaging.py`).
- The island is a disc whose nearest edge lies the chosen gap beyond the outer of the two main
  outlines, so it never overlaps them.
- Default radius 20 mm and island size are illustrative. The default tolerance, 4 mm, is the one the
  Decathlon used for its heart task [@antonelli2022].
- What would change the result: real errors are uneven along the outline, and 3-D surfaces weight
  regions by area.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Hausdorff distance reports the worst point; one island sets it.
- HD95 and ASSD summarize typical error; NSD reports the share within a chosen tolerance.
- State the tolerance and the percentile convention with every surface metric.

### What a boundary error costs

Suppose a segmentation is right in shape but its whole boundary sits $\delta$ too far out (or in).
The volume between the two surfaces is about $S\lvert\delta\rvert$, and Dice is
$1 - \lvert P \,\triangle\, T\rvert/(\lvert P\rvert+\lvert T\rvert)$, where $\triangle$ is the
symmetric difference. To first order in $\delta$,

$$
\mathrm{Dice} \approx 1 - \frac{\lvert\delta\rvert\, S}{2V}
$$ {#eq-m40-offset}

The loss scales with the surface-to-volume ratio $S/V$: large, round structures lose little; thin
or branched ones lose a lot. Two exact cases show the range. For concentric spheres of radii $R$
and $R + \delta$,

$$
\mathrm{Dice} = \frac{2\min(R, R+\delta)^3}{R^3 + (R+\delta)^3} \approx 1 - \frac{3\lvert\delta\rvert}{2R}
$$ {#eq-m40-sphere}

and for a wall of thickness $t$ shifted by $\delta$ along its normal,

$$
\mathrm{Dice} = \max\!\left(0,\; 1 - \frac{\lvert\delta\rvert}{t}\right)
$$ {#eq-m40-slab}

A 1-mm error on a sphere of radius 25 mm (illustrative, about the size of a blood pool) leaves Dice
at 0.94. The same error on a wall 1.89 mm thick, the mean measured by @beinart2011, leaves 0.47. A
Dice reported for the left atrial blood pool and one reported for its wall or for scar inside the
wall are therefore not on the same scale.

::: {.demo #m40-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m40-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m40-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m40-d2-structure-size.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Exact formulas: @eq-m40-sphere for the sphere, the same formula in two dimensions for a long
  cylinder grown radially, and @eq-m40-slab for the wall. The readout adds the first-order estimate of
  @eq-m40-offset for the sphere.
- The default wall thickness, 1.89 mm, and the slider range, 0.5 to 3.5 mm, are the mean and range
  measured on CT by @beinart2011. The sphere radius (25 mm) and cylinder radius (5 mm) are
  illustrative.
- What would change the result: real errors are not uniform, and real atria are neither spheres nor
  slabs (lab part E measures real atrial labels).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- For a uniform boundary error, Dice falls with surface-to-volume ratio (@eq-m40-offset).
- The same millimetre costs a thin wall far more than a blood pool.
- Compare Dice only between structures of similar shape and size.

### Risk models from images

Some imaging models predict when an event will happen rather than outline a structure. They are
judged by **Harrell's concordance index** [@harrell1982]. Take every pair of patients $(i, j)$
where $i$ had the event at time $t_i$ earlier than $j$'s follow-up time $t_j$; the model should give
$i$ the higher risk $r_i$:

$$
C = \frac{\sum_{i,j} \mathbb 1[t_i < t_j]\, e_i \left(\mathbb 1[r_i > r_j] + \tfrac12\, \mathbb 1[r_i = r_j]\right)}{\sum_{i,j} \mathbb 1[t_i < t_j]\, e_i}
$$ {#eq-m40-cindex}

where $e_i = 1$ if patient $i$ had the event. $C = 0.5$ is chance and $C = 1$ is perfect
ordering. $C$ measures ranking only: a model can order patients well and still predict the wrong
absolute risk, which calibration measures such as the integrated Brier score address. The deep
survival model of @popescu2022 reported both: $C$ of 0.83 and 0.74 and integrated Brier scores of
0.12 and 0.14 on internal validation and the independent test set.

**Key takeaways**

- $C$ is the share of comparable pairs a risk score orders correctly.
- Report calibration as well as $C$.
- Expect $C$ to drop on an independent cohort.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Fibrosis on MRI: from association to a randomized trial.** In the DECAAF cohort, atrial fibrosis
was quantified on delayed-enhancement MRI at a core laboratory before AF ablation in 15 centres
[@marrouche2014]. Of 329 enrolled patients, 57 were excluded for poor image quality. Each 1% more
fibrosis was associated with more recurrence (unadjusted hazard ratio 1.06 per 1%), and adding
fibrosis to clinical covariates raised the C statistic from 0.65 to 0.69.

DECAAF II then randomized 843 patients with persistent AF in 44 centres to pulmonary vein isolation
(PVI) plus ablation of MRI-defined fibrosis, or PVI alone [@marrouche2022]. Atrial arrhythmia
recurred in 43.0% and 46.1% (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17), not significantly different.
The safety composite occurred in 2.2% of the fibrosis-guided group and in none of the PVI group,
including 6 ischemic strokes in the fibrosis-guided group. A later analysis found that ablation
lesions did not uniformly produce scar on 3-month MRI, with large differences between centres
[@akoum2024].

**Shells and workflow.** For an AI-built left atrial shell from intracardiac echo, the published
comparison is with an earlier period of manual contouring at one centre [@zou2026]. It reports
shorter procedure and left atrial dwell times and similar 1-year freedom from AF.

In the terms of this module and m45:

- **An image-derived quantity can predict outcome without being a good target.** DECAAF showed an
  association; DECAAF II tested a treatment built on it and found no difference in recurrence.
- **Quantification depends on segmentation.** Fibrosis lives in a wall about 2 mm thick
  [@beinart2011], where a 1-mm boundary error removes half the overlap (@eq-m40-slab).
- **Before-and-after designs confound the tool with time.** Operators, workflows and patient mix
  change between periods; randomization, as in the echo trial of @he2023, separates them.

## How experts think

Before trusting an imaging model in an EP workflow, ask:

1. **Which structure, at what size?** A blood pool, a vein, a wall or scar inside the wall: the same
   error gives very different Dice (@eq-m40-offset, demo m40-d2).
2. **Which metrics, with which settings?** Dice for overlap, HD95 or ASSD for typical distance, NSD
   at a stated tolerance; Jaccard converted with @eq-m40-jaccard.
3. **Where are the errors?** Pulmonary veins, the appendage and the mitral plane are where outlines
   disagree (lab parts C and D); the benchmark of @tobongomez2015 standardized these regions before
   scoring.
4. **What does the error do downstream?** For a shell used with a map, measure the distance from
   touched points to the shell (lab part D), not only Dice.
5. **Was a decision tested, or only an association?** DECAAF and DECAAF II answer different
   questions [@marrouche2014; @marrouche2022].

One sentence to keep: **a segmentation score means something only for a named structure, a named
metric and a named use.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Dice and Jaccard (@eq-m40-jaccard) | $\mathrm{Dice} = 2J/(1+J)$, $J = \mathrm{Dice}/(2-\mathrm{Dice})$ |
| Hausdorff distance (@eq-m40-hausdorff) | Largest point-to-surface distance, both directions; HD95 uses the 95th percentile |
| ASSD (@eq-m40-assd) | Mean surface-to-surface distance, both directions |
| NSD (@eq-m40-nsd) | Share of both surfaces within $\tau$ of the other |
| Boundary offset (@eq-m40-offset) | $\mathrm{Dice} \approx 1 - \lvert\delta\rvert S/(2V)$ |
| Spheres (@eq-m40-sphere) | $2\min(R,R+\delta)^3/(R^3+(R+\delta)^3) \approx 1 - 3\lvert\delta\rvert/(2R)$ |
| Shifted wall (@eq-m40-slab) | $\max(0, 1 - \lvert\delta\rvert/t)$ |
| Concordance (@eq-m40-cindex) | Share of comparable pairs ordered correctly; 0.5 is chance |

**Studies in this module**

| Study | What was done | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @xiong2020 | Left atrium on late-gadolinium MRI, 27 teams | Open benchmark |
| @antonelli2022 | Ten segmentation tasks, including the left atrium | Open benchmark |
| @popescu2022 | Arrhythmic death risk from scar on MRI | Internal validation and independent test set |
| @zou2026 | AI-built left atrial shell from intracardiac echo | Single-centre before-and-after |
| @marrouche2022 | Strategy: MRI-fibrosis ablation plus PVI vs PVI | Randomized trial |
| @he2023 | AI vs sonographer first read of ejection fraction (echo) | Blinded randomized trial |

**Rules of thumb**

- Always pair an overlap metric with a distance metric.
- Report surface metrics per region (body, veins, appendage) when the use depends on them.
- Find the region of interest first: in the left atrial benchmark, two-stage networks did best
  [@xiong2020]; lab part E shows why.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. A paper reports an intersection over union of 0.80; another reports a Dice of 0.86. Which is
better?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Convert first (@eq-m40-jaccard): $J = 0.80$ is a Dice of $1.6/1.8 = 0.889$, higher than 0.86. Then
check that both used the same structure, data set and label protocol; otherwise the comparison is
still not fair.

</details>

**Q2. A segmentation has Dice 0.95 but a Hausdorff distance of 30 mm. What happened?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Most likely a small false island or a stray protrusion far from the structure. It costs little
volume, so Dice barely moves, but the Hausdorff distance is a maximum and reports the worst
point (@eq-m40-hausdorff; demo m40-d1). Look at HD95, the island itself, and whether a largest-component
step would remove it.

</details>

**Q3. When would you report HD95, ASSD or NSD?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

HD95 for a near-worst-case distance that ignores a few outliers; ASSD for the typical error over the
whole surface (@eq-m40-assd); NSD when there is a clinically meaningful tolerance, for example the
distance within which a shell is usable for guidance (@eq-m40-nsd). State the percentile convention
and the tolerance, since toolkits differ.

</details>

**Q4. What does NSD at 4 mm of 0.95 mean?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

95% of the two surfaces, counted together, lie within 4 mm of the other surface. It says nothing
about how far the remaining 5% are; pair it with HD95 or the Hausdorff distance. The Decathlon used
4 mm for its heart task [@antonelli2022].

</details>

**Q5. Why does the same 1-mm error give Dice 0.94 for a blood pool and 0.47 for the atrial wall?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Dice loss scales with surface-to-volume ratio (@eq-m40-offset). A sphere of radius 25 mm loses about
$3 \times 1/(2 \times 25) = 6\%$ (@eq-m40-sphere); a wall 1.89 mm thick shifted by 1 mm keeps only
$1 - 1/1.89 = 0.47$ (@eq-m40-slab). Thin structures need distance metrics or a much finer grid.

</details>

**Q6. Can you compare the Dice of a left atrial blood-pool model with that of a scar model?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

No. Scar lies inside a wall about 2 mm thick [@beinart2011] and forms small, irregular regions, so
its surface-to-volume ratio is much higher, and @eq-m40-offset predicts a lower Dice for the same
boundary error. Compare each against its own baseline, such as agreement between two human raters
on the same images.

</details>

**Q7. How would you validate an automatically built atrial shell for use with a mapping system?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Compare with a reference shell on held-out patients using Dice, HD95, ASSD and NSD at a tolerance
agreed with users; report errors per region (veins, appendage, mitral plane), where outlines differ
most [@tobongomez2015]. Then measure the distance from catheter contact points to the shell (lab
part D). Finally, test the workflow: time, safety and outcome, ideally randomized.

</details>

**Q8. A survival model has a concordance index of 0.74. What does that tell you, and what not?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In 74% of comparable pairs, the patient with the earlier event had the higher predicted
risk (@eq-m40-cindex). It says nothing about calibration (whether a predicted 10% risk means 10%) or about
benefit from acting on the score. In @popescu2022, $C$ fell from 0.83 on internal validation to 0.74
on the independent test set, and the authors note that the two cohorts differ.

</details>

**Q9. DECAAF found fibrosis predicted recurrence; DECAAF II found fibrosis-guided ablation did not
reduce it. Is that a contradiction?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

No. A marker can predict outcome without being a target whose ablation changes outcome
[@marrouche2014; @marrouche2022]. The trial also found more safety events in the fibrosis-guided
group, and a later analysis showed that lesions did not uniformly become scar [@akoum2024].
Association and intervention are different questions.

</details>

**Q10. What could bias a before-and-after comparison of AI-built and manually built shells?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Anything else that changed between periods: operator experience (learning curve), other workflow or
equipment changes, patient selection, and follow-up practice. The study design of @zou2026 compares a
later period with an earlier one, so differences cannot be attributed to the AI alone. Randomization
or a stepped design, with blinded outcome assessment, would separate them.

</details>

**Q11. What made the AI-versus-sonographer echo trial a strong design?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Studies were randomized to an AI or a sonographer first read, cardiologists who finalized the
reports could not tell which they had (blinding index 0.088), and the primary endpoint was the share
of studies whose ejection fraction the cardiologist changed by more than 5% [@he2023]. It also reports what
it did not test: long-term patient outcomes.

</details>

**Q12. In lab part E, the same voxel classifier does well in a tight box and badly in a loose one.
Why, and what does that say about real pipelines?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Local intensity features cannot tell the left atrium from other blood pools; in a tight box there are
few other blood pools, in a loose box there are several, and the largest component may be the wrong
one. Real pipelines need a localization step, and its errors count. The left atrial benchmark found
that two-stage networks (localize, then segment) did best [@xiong2020]. The tight box in the lab is
taken from the label, so it is an optimistic "oracle" first stage.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab computes segmentation metrics on shapes with known answers, segments synthetic atria with a
threshold and a voxel classifier, measures what the errors mean for points on the wall, and repeats
the key measurements on 20 real left atrial labels. Parts A to D run in under a minute.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Metrics with known answers: @eq-m40-sphere, @eq-m40-slab, an island and the Hausdorff distance | synthetic |
| B | Synthetic atria: body, veins, appendage, a bright neighbour, bias and noise | synthetic |
| C | Threshold against a voxel classifier; Dice, HD95, ASSD and NSD; body against veins | synthetic |
| D | From mask to map: distance from points on the true wall to the predicted shell | synthetic |
| E | Real left atrial labels: shape, boundary errors, islands, and a classifier in a tight or loose box | MSD Task02_Heart |
| F | Optional: a 2-D U-Net in PyTorch (MONAI's implementation if installed) | synthetic |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m40_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m40_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m40_lab.ipynb).
- **Data for part E:** the 20 labelled training volumes of the Medical Segmentation Decathlon heart
  task [@antonelli2022], from the 2013 Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge [@tobongomez2015], licence
  CC BY-SA 4.0. The archive is downloaded from the MONAI consortium's AWS Open Data bucket and checked
  against the MD5 value MONAI publishes; nothing derived from it is stored in this repository. Without
  internet access, part E is skipped.
- **Part F** runs only if PyTorch is installed; it uses MONAI [@cardoso2022monai] when available.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A Jaccard index of 0.5. What is the Dice?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2 \times 0.5/1.5 = 0.67$ (@eq-m40-jaccard).

</details>

**S2. A sphere of radius 20 mm is segmented 1 mm too large all round. Estimate Dice.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About $1 - 3/40 = 0.925$ from the first-order form; the exact value is 0.927 (@eq-m40-sphere).

</details>

**S3. A wall 2 mm thick is segmented 1 mm off along its normal. Dice?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

0.5 (@eq-m40-slab).

</details>

**S4. The prediction equals the truth plus one voxel 30 mm away. What happens to Dice and to the
Hausdorff distance?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Dice barely changes; the Hausdorff distance becomes 30 mm (@eq-m40-hausdorff).

</details>

**S5. Every point of both surfaces lies within 2 mm of the other surface. What is NSD at 2 mm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1 (@eq-m40-nsd).

</details>

**S6. A risk score is pure noise. What concordance index do you expect? And if it ranks patients in
exactly the wrong order?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

About 0.5; and 0 (@eq-m40-cindex).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Ten tasks, one benchmark.** Antonelli and colleagues, Fig. 1, the overview of the ten
  Decathlon tasks and the difficulty each was chosen for, including the small heart data set
  [@antonelli2022; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9287542/)]. This
  module: From the field; lab part E.
- **A survival curve per patient.** Popescu and colleagues, Extended Data Fig. 2, predicted survival
  curves for one patient who had arrhythmic sudden death and one who did not, drawn against
  Kaplan–Meier and Cox-model curves [@popescu2022;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9022904/)]. Compare with what the
  concordance index does and does not measure (@eq-m40-cindex, interview Q8).
- **A trial flow for an imaging AI.** He and colleagues, the study flow figure, which shows the
  echocardiograms excluded for image quality before randomization [@he2023;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10115627/)]. Compare with the
  before-and-after design of the clinical correlate (interview Q10, Q11).

## Further reading

- **Metrics.** @maierhein2024 (Metrics Reloaded) and @reinke2024 (metric pitfalls).
- **Benchmarks and methods.** @tobongomez2015, @xiong2020, @antonelli2022 and its preprint with
  per-task results [@antonelli2021msd], @ronneberger2015 (U-Net), @isensee2021 (nnU-Net).
- **Open tools.** @cardoso2022monai (MONAI), @diazpinto2022monailabel (MONAI Label).
- **Imaging and risk.** @popescu2022, @razeghi2023.
- **Fibrosis and ablation.** @marrouche2014, @marrouche2022, @akoum2024.
- **Echo AI from Stanford.** @ouyang2020, @he2023.
